docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Posting 3 is a rewrite of Posting in Go, available as a public beta. It installs as a single binary and adds GraphQL, gRPC, request tabs, layered environments, request timing, and remote control.

You can open your existing Posting 2 HTTP collections without converting them. Configuration, keymaps, and themes have some differences, and Python scripts aren't run.

Sharing a collection with Posting 2

Ordinary HTTP requests use the shared .posting.yaml format, but Posting 3 adds fields that Posting 2 doesn't understand. Saving a request in Posting 2 removes kind, graphql, grpc, and variable_scope, losing the query, RPC settings, or scoped variables stored there. Edit GraphQL, gRPC, and requests with scoped variables only in Posting 3.

docs.title: What carries over
docs.text: Collections Posting 3 opens Posting 2 collections. Ordinary HTTP requests without Posting 3 fields can be edited in either version. Configuration Posting 3 reads the same config.yaml and POSTING_* environment variables. A few settings aren't supported yet; see Configuration. Environment files .env files work as before, and --env still accepts file paths. The default collection Posting 3 uses the same default collection directory. Keymaps Action IDs are the same where the action still exists. See Keymaps for the differences. Themes Posting 2 theme files with hex colours are loaded, using their main colours. See Themes from Posting 2.

docs.title: What's new
docs.text:
• GraphQL requests. Edit a query and its JSON variables, choose an operation, and see GraphQL errors even when the HTTP status is 200.
  • gRPC requests. Discover methods through reflection or local proto files, send unary and streaming calls, and keep a stream open to send messages as you work.
  • Request tabs. Open as many requests as you like, each in its own tab, and send them at the same time. Browsing the collection uses a single preview tab, so tabs don't pile up.
  • Layered environments. A shared posting.env base, per-environment files like staging.env, and .local.env files for secrets that stay out of version control. Start in one by name with --env staging. Posting remembers the environment you switch to in each collection, and starts in it next time.
  • Request timing. The Trace tab shows how long each stage of an exchange took, and the URL bar shows its progress while it's in flight. Timing is kept in history too.
  • Collection search. Press Ctrl+G to filter the collection as you type, by name, folder or method.
  • Curl export with or without variables. Export a request as a curl command that's ready to run, or one that keeps its ${VARIABLES} for sharing.
  • Coding agents. Claude Code, Codex and other agents can send requests through the Posting you have open with posting remote, so you watch what they send and what comes back. Install the using-posting skill to teach them how.
  • Bruno import. posting import now reads Bruno requests and collections, and detects the format of any source by itself.
  • 37 themes, previewed live as you browse them.
  • Resizable panels. Drag the dividers between the sidebar, request and response.
  • Remote control. Use posting remote from another terminal or a coding agent to open, send, and save requests in the running app, using its active environment. Run posting remote --help for the command reference.

docs.title: What's changed
docs.text:
• Installation. Posting 3 is installed with Homebrew, from a release download or with go install. Updating a uv or pipx installation keeps you on Posting 2. See Installation.
  • Some shortcuts moved. Searching requests is now Ctrl+G, and expanding a panel is Alt+Z. Ctrl+N opens a new request tab.
  • Help. F1 shows all the keyboard shortcuts in one place, rather than help for the focused widget.
  • History is stored separately in a new format. Posting 2 history isn't shown or removed.
  • Configuration. POSTING_* settings are read from the shell environment, not from request .env files. Custom CA bundles must be PEM files, rather than directories of certificates. See Configuration for supported settings.
  • The theme picker previews themes as you move through them. Posting 2 themes that no longer exist fall back to galaxy.

docs.title: Not yet supported
docs.text:
These Posting 2 features aren't in Posting 3 yet:

  • Scripts. Pre-request and post-response Python scripts aren't run. They're kept in your request files, so nothing is lost. See Scripting for alternatives.
  • X resources themes (use_xresources), and live reloading of theme files (watch_themes).
  • Custom syntax highlighting and method colours in theme files. Colours come from the theme's main colours instead.

You can keep Posting 2 installed alongside Posting 3 for HTTP requests that need these features. Follow the sharing restrictions above when you use the same collection in both versions. Both install a command called posting, so whichever comes first on your PATH wins. Run the other by its full path, or give it an alias in your shell.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Posting is designed to be driven from the keyboard, but everything can be clicked too.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
From top to bottom, Posting's screen is made up of:

  • The sidebar, on the left, running the full height of the screen. It has two tabs: Requests, the requests in your collection, and History, the responses you've received.
  • The header, a single row showing the active environment and your user@host. Click the environment's name to switch to another.
  • The request tabs, one for each request you have open.
  • The URL bar, with the method selector on its left.
  • The Request panel, where you edit the request's headers, body, parameters, auth and options.
  • The Response panel, which shows the response. It sits below the request, or beside it in the side by side layout.
  • The footer, showing the most useful keys for whatever has focus.

The dividers between the sidebar and the panels, and between the request and response, can be dragged with the mouse to resize them.

docs.title: Changing the layout
docs.text:
A few commands in the command palette (Ctrl+P) change the layout for the rest of the session:

  • Layout: side by side / Layout: stacked puts the response beside or below the request.
  • View: hide collection / View: show collection hides or shows the sidebar. Ctrl+H does the same.
  • View: expand request / View: expand response makes one panel fill the screen. Alt+Z expands the Request or Response panel, whichever has focus (the Request panel if neither does), and pressing it again restores both.

To make any of these permanent, set layout, collection_browser.show_on_startup or collection_browser.position in your configuration.

Jump mode is the fastest way to get around.

Press Ctrl+O and a label appears over every part of the screen you can move to. Type a label to jump straight there. Press Esc to leave jump mode without moving.

Some labels are always the same, so they soon become muscle memory:

Label Jumps to 1 The method selector 2 The URL bar 3 The requests in the collection 4 The history list Q W E R T Y U The request tabs: Headers, Body, Path, Query, Auth, Info and Options. docs.title: Moving around with the keyboard
docs.text:
• Tab and Shift+Tab move focus forward and backward through the fields on screen.
  • The arrow keys (or H J K L where you're not typing) move within a part of the screen, and between neighbouring parts where it makes sense. For example, Down in the URL bar moves into the request tabs, Down from a tab moves into its content, and Up from the top of a tab's content moves back to the tabs.
  • Ctrl+L jumps to the URL bar from anywhere, and Ctrl+T opens the method menu.

docs.title: Request tabs
docs.text:
Every request you open gets a tab above the URL bar. Each tab shows the request's method and name. A dot (●) marks a tab with unsaved changes, and … marks a tab whose request is being sent.

Key Action Ctrl+N Open a new, empty request tab Alt+Right / Alt+Left Go to the next / previous tab Alt+Down Search your open tabs by name Alt+W Close the current tab

You can also click a tab to switch to it, click its ✕ to close it, click + for a new tab, or click ▾ to search your tabs. When there are more tabs than fit, scroll the strip with the mouse wheel, or click the ‹ and › arrows at its ends.

Warning

Closing a tab doesn't ask for confirmation, even if it has unsaved changes.

Each tab sends its own requests. You can send a slow request, move to another tab, and carry on working: when the response arrives it's kept in its tab, and Posting doesn't pull you away from what you're doing. Press Esc to cancel a request that's in flight.

docs.title: Preview tabs
docs.text:
When you open a request from the collection or from history, it opens in a preview tab, whose name is shown in italics. Opening another request replaces the preview tab instead of opening yet another tab, so you can browse through your collection without leaving a trail of tabs behind.

The preview tab becomes an ordinary tab, which stays open, as soon as you:

  • edit the request, send it, or save it
  • double-click its tab, or double-click the request in the collection
  • choose Keep tab open from the command palette

If a request is already open in a tab, opening it again takes you to that tab.

docs.title: Searching for requests
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+G from anywhere to search the requests in your collection. You can also press / while the collection has focus. The collection is filtered as you type:

  • Separate words with spaces. Every word must match part of a request's name or folder, or the start of its method, so post users finds POST requests in a users folder.
  • Press Enter or Down to move into the results, and Enter to open a request.
  • Press Esc to clear the search.

docs.title: Mouse support
docs.text:
Anything you can focus with the keyboard can be clicked. A few things are only a click away:

  • Hovering over a request in the collection shows its description, if it has one.
  • Clicking the environment name in the header opens the environment switcher.
  • Clicking the Posting logo in the bottom left corner opens a menu with links to these docs, sponsoring the project, and Mastodon.
  • Clicking wrap on/wrap off or copy under the response body toggles line wrapping or copies the body.

docs.title: Focus settings
docs.text:
Three settings choose where the cursor goes at key moments:

Setting Values Default focus.on_startup url, method, collection url focus.on_request_open url, method, headers, body, path, query, info Focus doesn't move focus.on_response body, tabs Focus doesn't move

For example, to jump into the response body whenever a response arrives:

focus:
  on_response: body

focus.on_response only applies to the tab you're looking at: a response for a tab in the background never moves the cursor.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Press F1 at any time to see the keyboard shortcuts, including any you've changed in your keymap. See Help for more ways to find your way around.

docs.title: Quitting
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C, or choose Quit Posting from the command palette.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
posting remote drives the Posting you have open from another terminal. A request sent with posting remote send opens and sends in Posting's window, using its active environment, so you watch the request and its response arrive. The response is also printed in the terminal the command ran in.

It's made for working beside a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex: run the agent in one pane and Posting in another, and the agent can call your API through Posting while you watch. It can use the requests and environments you already have, and everything it sends lands in your History.

posting remote requests                  # what's in the collection
posting remote send users/list           # send a saved request
posting remote send --curl 'curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users -d "{}"'
posting remote response --json           # the active tab's latest response

Run posting remote --help for the full reference. It is written so an agent can learn the command from it.

To teach your coding agent to use Posting this way, install the using-posting skill. See Coding Agents.

To let an agent run saved requests or entire collections without a running Posting, use posting run instead. Its JSON output includes responses for the agent to inspect.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command What it does list List the running Postings. requests List the requests saved in the collection. show Print the request in the active tab, in Posting's request file format. open [REQUEST] Open a request in a tab, without sending it. send [REQUEST] Send a request, wait for the response, and print it. response Print the active tab's latest response. env [NAME\|FILE...] List the environments, after switching to the one named, or to the files given. --none switches to no environment. save [FILE] Save the request in the active tab. --name NAME names it.

docs.title: Choosing a request
docs.text:
open and send take a request saved in the collection: its file (users/get.posting.yaml, or just users/get), a path to the file, or the request's name. A saved request opens just as it would from the sidebar: in its own tab if it's already open, unsaved edits and all, and otherwise in the preview tab.

Instead of a saved request, give one of:

  • --curl COMMAND: a curl command, imported as if pasted into the URL bar.
  • --yaml FILE: a request in Posting's YAML format. --yaml - reads it from standard input. A path to a request file outside the collection works the same way.

Requests that aren't saved open in a tab of their own, which later ones reuse, so a string of them doesn't fill the tab strip. Once you edit or save that tab it's yours, and the next request gets a new tab.

With no request given, open and send use the active tab, so posting remote send sends whatever you have open.

A handy loop for changing a request is to print it, edit it, and send the result:

posting remote show > draft.posting.yaml
# edit draft.posting.yaml
posting remote send --yaml draft.posting.yaml

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
posting remote env lists the environments Posting can switch to, marking the active one with *, along with the names of their variables. Values aren't shown, since they're often secrets.

posting remote env              # list them
posting remote env staging      # switch to staging, then list them
posting remote env --none       # switch to no environment

Give a name from the list, or one or more .env files to layer. Switching from the command line is shown in Posting, but isn't remembered for the next launch: which environment Posting starts in stays your choice.

docs.title: Saving requests
docs.text:
posting remote save saves the request in the active tab, so a request built from the command line can join the collection:

posting remote open --curl 'curl https://api.example.com/health'
posting remote save ops/health --name "Health check"

FILE is relative to the collection unless it starts with /, ./ or ../, and .posting.yaml is added if it's missing. Without FILE, a request that's already saved is saved in place, and an unsaved one is saved in the collection's top folder under its name. save never replaces a different request that's already saved.

save acts on the active tab, so if you have unsaved edits open there, they're what gets saved.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
send and response print the response the way curl -i does: the status line, the headers, a blank line, then the body. JSON bodies are indented. With --json, every command prints its result as JSON instead, which suits scripts and agents:

posting remote send users/get --json | jq -r .response.body

An error status such as 404 is still a response: send exits 0 when a response arrives, and 1 when none does, for example when the server can't be reached or a variable isn't defined. The error is printed on standard error.

docs.title: Several Postings at once
docs.text: Each Posting listens for commands while it runs. When more than one is running, posting remote picks the one started in the current directory, or else the one whose collection contains the current directory or is inside it. To choose one yourself, give its process ID (from posting remote list) with --instance, or set POSTING_INSTANCE.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Posting listens on a Unix socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/posting, or in a directory of your own in the system's temporary directory. The directory is accessible only to you, and Posting refuses to use one that belongs to anyone else. Nothing listens on the network.

To turn remote control off, set remote_control.enabled to false in your configuration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A request is everything Posting needs to make an HTTP call: the method and URL, headers, query and path parameters, a body, authentication and a few options. You edit a request in the Request panel, send it with Ctrl+J, and save it into your collection with Ctrl+S.

docs.title: Creating a request
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+N to open a new, empty request in a tab of its own. Choose a method with Ctrl+T (or press a method's letter while the method selector has focus: G GET, P POST, U PUT, A PATCH, D DELETE, H HEAD, O OPTIONS), and type a URL.

You don't need to type https:// or http://: a URL without a scheme is sent over http://.

A new request isn't written to disk until you save it.

docs.title: Editing a request
docs.text:
The Request panel has seven tabs. Jump to any of them with Ctrl+O followed by Q W E R T Y U, or move along the tabs with Left and Right and press Down to move into one.

Type $ in the URL bar, a header, query or form value, the auth fields, the proxy URL or the body to see the variables you can use. See Environments for how variables work.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Headers are edited in a table. Type into the empty row at the bottom to add a header, and another empty row appears beneath it. As you type a header's name, Posting suggests common header names.

Key Action Up / Down Move between rows Ctrl+R Enable or disable the row Ctrl+X Delete the row

You can also click the checkbox at the start of a row to enable or disable it, or the ✕ at its end to delete it. A disabled row stays in the request, and is saved with it, but isn't sent. The Query and form tables work the same way. The Path table only has values to fill in: its rows come from the URL (see Path).

docs.title: Body
docs.text:
Choose the kind of body with the selector at the top of the tab (Left and Right change it):

  • None sends no body.
  • Raw sends the text you type. Choose its content type beside it: JSON, Text, XML or HTML. The text is syntax highlighted, and Posting sends the matching Content-Type header, unless you've set a Content-Type header yourself.
  • Form sends URL-encoded form fields (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), edited in a table.
  • Multipart sends an ordered mixture of text and file parts (multipart/form-data).
  • File sends a file's bytes as the entire body, without multipart framing, for example for a PUT upload.

Press F4 in the body to edit it in your own editor, or F3 to view it in your pager. See External Tools.

docs.title: Multipart and file uploads
docs.text:
In Multipart, select a part in the list to edit its details beside it. On a narrow pane, Enter opens the details full-width and Esc returns to the list. Choose + Add part or press Ins to add one. Use Ctrl+R to enable or disable the selected part, Ctrl+X to delete it, and Alt+Up / Alt+Down to reorder it. Disabled parts are saved but not sent. Repeated names are kept: to send several files as attachments, add a part for each file with that name.

A Text part has a multiline value and an optional content type, for example application/json for metadata. F4 and F3 work in its value. A File part has a path, an optional filename override, and an optional content type. With no overrides, Posting sends the basename as the filename and infers the content type from the extension, falling back to application/octet-stream. Switching part types or body modes keeps drafts in the open tab; only the selected body mode and part type are written to YAML.

Paths are relative to the collection root, including for unsaved requests, or absolute. They refer to files on the machine running Posting: over SSH, these are files on the remote host. Type a path to see directory and file completions, then press Enter to accept one. Suggestions use up to 512 entries in each directory; you can always type an exact path. F5 in the path refreshes its metadata. Posting supports regular files, including empty files, not directories, devices, stdin or glob patterns.

Substitute body variables applies to part names, text values, paths, filenames and content types. It never changes file contents. Importing and saving store references, not file bytes. Each send reads the current files, so re-sending a history entry is not a replay of historical file contents. Keep shared fixtures in the collection, or use variables for machine-specific paths.

Posting checks every enabled file before connecting. It streams uploads, shows byte progress, then waits for the response. Esc cancels the request. Redirects and Digest authentication can resend the body; if a file's identity, size or modification time changed, Posting stops and asks you to send again. The request timeout includes uploading, so increase it for large files.

Posting generates the multipart boundary and its Content-Type. Leave that header unset, or use bare multipart/form-data; a different type or a manually supplied boundary is an error.

For example:

body:
  multipart:
    - name: title
      value: ${TITLE}
    - name: document
      file: fixtures/report.pdf
    - name: metadata
      value: '{"team":"finance"}'
      content_type: application/json

For a whole-file body, use body: {file: fixtures/report.pdf} with an optional content_type. Each multipart part has exactly one of value or file, plus optional filename, content_type and enabled: false. Multipart and file bodies require Posting 3; older versions cannot preserve them.

docs.title: Path
docs.text:
Path parameters are placeholders in the URL's path, written as :name:

https://api.example.com/users/:id/comments/:commentId

Each placeholder you type in the URL gets a row in the Path tab, where you fill in its value. The rows come from the URL, so you add or remove them by editing the URL. Values are inserted into the URL when the request is sent. A placeholder with an empty value is sent as it is.

Values can contain variables, such as $USER_ID.

To send a literal :name in a path, double the colon: ::name is sent as :name.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
The Query tab lists the query string's parameters, and it's kept in step with the URL. Type ?page=2&per_page=50 at the end of the URL and two rows appear in the Query tab; add, change or remove rows and the URL updates to match.

A disabled row is kept in the Query tab but removed from the URL, so it isn't sent.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Choose how the request authenticates:

  • None sends no credentials.
  • Basic sends a username and password with HTTP Basic authentication.
  • Digest answers the server's Digest challenge with a username and password.
  • Bearer token sends Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • OAuth 2.0 obtains and refreshes a bearer token using authorization code with PKCE or client credentials.

The Authorization header is created when the request is sent, and replaces any Authorization header you've added yourself (for Digest auth, once the server has sent its challenge). Credentials can use variables, for example ${API_TOKEN}, so you can keep secrets out of your request files.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Choose OAuth 2.0 in Auth, then choose a grant:

  • Code + PKCE signs in through your browser. Enter the provider's Auth URL, Token URL, Client ID, and space-separated Scopes. Public clients leave Client secret empty. Register http://127.0.0.1:8765/oauth/callback as a redirect URI with the provider, or enter another HTTP loopback IP, port and path in Redirect URI. Posting uses S256 PKCE and checks the callback's state. Request the provider's offline-access scope, often offline_access, if needed to receive a refresh token.
  • Client credentials authenticates an application without a browser. Enter the Token URL, Client ID, Client secret and any Scopes the provider requires.

Client auth chooses how Posting sends client credentials to the token endpoint: Body (client_secret_post, the default) or Basic header (client_secret_basic). Public PKCE clients use Body with no secret. Follow your provider's client registration settings.

Press Ctrl+J to authorize and send. A code grant opens the browser and waits up to three minutes; Esc cancels it. The browser must be able to reach the callback on the machine running Posting. When using SSH or a container, forward the callback port if the browser is on another machine. Port 0 selects an available port, for providers that permit variable loopback ports. The API request's timeout starts after authorization finishes.

Posting reuses tokens and refreshes them shortly before expiry, on the next send. It keeps a rotated refresh token when the provider returns one. Client credentials grants obtain a new token instead. A revoked or expired refresh token needs a new login: choose Forget OAuth token in the command palette, then send again. Forgetting removes the token for the current configuration from memory and the credential store; it doesn't revoke consent at the provider. Posting doesn't automatically replay API requests that return 401.

Tokens are saved in the OS credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or a Linux Secret Service such as GNOME Keyring. On Linux this requires an available, unlocked store on the session D-Bus. If the store is unavailable, Posting warns in Auth and keeps the token in memory for this session only; it never falls back to a plaintext token file. Tokens are scoped to the collection, API origin and resolved OAuth configuration, so changing credentials or scopes doesn't reuse another configuration's token.

Use variables such as ${CLIENT_SECRET} for secrets. Literal client credentials are saved in request YAML, just like Basic auth credentials. Generated access and refresh tokens aren't written to request files, request history configurations, or YAML exports. API responses are still recorded normally, so don't use an endpoint that echoes credentials if you want them kept out of response history. OAuth requests can't be exported as curl or grpcurl commands.

OAuth endpoints and HTTP API requests require HTTPS, except HTTP on loopback for local testing. Token requests use the request's proxy and SSL verification settings and the configured CA/client certificates. Token endpoint redirects aren't followed, and API redirects to a different origin don't receive the OAuth token. OAuth also works with GraphQL and TLS gRPC calls. gRPC reflection can reuse or refresh credentials but doesn't open a browser; send once to sign in first.

A saved OAuth request looks like this:

url: https://api.example.com/me
auth:
  type: oauth2
  oauth2:
    grant_type: authorization_code
    authorization_url: https://identity.example.com/authorize
    token_url: https://identity.example.com/token
    client_id: ${CLIENT_ID}
    scope: openid profile offline_access
    redirect_uri: http://127.0.0.1:8765/oauth/callback
    client_auth: client_secret_post

For client credentials, use grant_type: client_credentials, add client_secret: ${CLIENT_SECRET}, and omit authorization_url and redirect_uri. Edit OAuth requests only in Posting 3; Posting 2 doesn't understand this auth type.

docs.title: Info
docs.text:
The request's Name and Description, and the File it's saved in.

The name is shown in the request tabs and the collection browser. The description is shown when you hover over the request in the collection browser, and supports code in backticks.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description Follow redirects On Follow 3xx responses to their destination, stopping with an error after 10 requests in a chain. When it's off, you see the redirect response itself. Verify SSL certificates On Reject servers whose certificates can't be verified. Turn it off for servers with self-signed certificates. See also Configuring SSL. Attach cookies On Send cookies set by earlier responses, and remember cookies from this one. Cookies are kept until you quit Posting, and are shared by all tabs. Substitute body variables On Replace variables in the body. Turn this off to send a body that contains literal $ signs, such as a JSON schema or a GraphQL query. Variables in the URL, headers and auth are still replaced. Proxy URL Empty Send the request through this proxy, e.g. http://proxy.example.com:8080. When it's empty, the standard HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables apply. Timeout 5 How many seconds to wait for the whole request, including redirects and reading the response.

docs.title: GraphQL requests
docs.text:
To make a GraphQL request, open the method selector with Ctrl+T and choose GraphQL, or press Q while the method selector has focus. The selector shows GraphQL, and the collection browser, request tabs and history show a GQL badge where an HTTP request shows its method. Choose a method to turn it back into an HTTP request. The URL, headers, auth and options stay as they are when you switch, and so does the query, so you can switch back and forth without losing anything.

A GraphQL request has two tabs of its own, before the usual ones:

  • Query holds the GraphQL document, with syntax highlighting. If the document defines more than one operation, type the name of the one to run in Operation, above the document.
  • Variables holds the operation's variables as a JSON object, such as {"id": "${USER_ID}"}.

The other tabs work as they do for an HTTP request. There's no Body tab, and the URL's query parameters are in the Params tab, because Query is the document. Press F4 in the document or the variables to edit them in your own editor.

Posting sends a GraphQL request as a POST with Content-Type: application/json and a JSON body of query, variables and operationName. Empty variables and an empty operation name are left out. Unless you've set an Accept header, Posting also sends Accept: application/graphql-response+json, application/json.

docs.title: Variables in GraphQL requests
docs.text:
In the Variables tab, Posting variables work as they do in a raw body: $NAME and ${NAME} are both replaced, and typing $ suggests the variables you can use.

In the query, only ${NAME} is replaced. A bare $name there is a GraphQL variable, so query User($id: ID!) is sent as written, even if your environment defines id.

Turn off Substitute body variables in the Options tab to send the query and the variables exactly as written.

docs.title: GraphQL responses
docs.text: GraphQL servers often answer 200 OK when an operation fails, and put the failure in an errors list in the response body. When a 2xx response has errors, Posting shows its status in the warning colour, in the URL bar, the response panel and the history, and the response panel counts the errors, for example 200 1 error.

docs.title: GraphQL request files
docs.text:
A saved GraphQL request has kind: graphql and a graphql section instead of a method and a body:

name: Get user
kind: graphql
url: ${BASE_URL}/graphql
graphql:
  query: |
    query User($id: ID!) {
      user(id: $id) {
        name
        email
      }
    }
  variables: |
    {"id": "${USER_ID}"}
  operation_name: User
auth:
  type: bearer_token
  bearer_token:
    token: ${API_TOKEN}

Posting 2 doesn't know about GraphQL requests. It opens them as a GET of the URL with no body, and saving one in Posting 2 removes kind and the graphql section, which loses the query. Edit GraphQL requests only in Posting 3.

docs.title: WebSocket requests
docs.text:
Choose WebSocket in the method selector (Ctrl+T, then W). Enter a ws:// or wss:// URL and press Connect or Ctrl+J. Connecting does not send the draft in the Message tab. Once connected, Send or Ctrl+J sends that draft as one message. Edit it and send again as often as needed, including empty messages. Enable Binary (base64) to send base64-decoded bytes instead of UTF-8 text.

The Messages response tab shows sent and received messages with timestamps. JSON messages use the existing text and JSON tree inspectors; binary messages are shown as base64. New messages appear without keyboard or mouse activity. Select an older message to pause following while new messages accumulate; F resumes following. Enter opens the full inspector and Esc returns to the log without disconnecting.

Press Alt+J or choose Disconnect WebSocket to disconnect. Esc from the log also disconnects. The log, handshake headers, close code and reason remain available in history. Unsent queued messages are discarded on disconnect. Reconnection is explicit and never replays messages. The request timeout bounds connecting and each write; it does not end an established interactive connection. A caller's deadline still applies.

Headers, query/path parameters, Basic/Bearer/OAuth authentication, cookies, proxy and TLS settings apply to the upgrade handshake. To offer subprotocols, add a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header. OAuth requires wss:// except on loopback. Ping frames receive automatic pong replies. Redirects, Digest authentication, per-message compression and automatic reconnect are not supported. Messages are limited to 1 MiB; the connection stops when the retained log reaches 10,000 entries or 64 MiB of payloads, preserving the log and explaining the limit.

Saved requests use kind: websocket:

name: Deployment updates
kind: websocket
url: wss://api.example.com/events
websocket:
  message: '{"subscribe":"deployments"}'
  binary: false

Edit these files only in Posting 3. Export as YAML is supported; command export is not. See headless WebSocket runs for the different send/timeout behavior of posting run.

docs.title: gRPC requests
docs.text: To make a gRPC request, open the method selector with Ctrl+T and choose gRPC, or press R while the method selector has focus. The selector shows gRPC, and the collection browser, request tabs and history show an RPC badge where an HTTP request shows its method. Choose a method to turn it back into an HTTP request. The address, metadata, auth and options stay as they are when you switch, and so do the gRPC method and message.

docs.title: The server's address
docs.text:
Type the server's address in the URL bar, for example localhost:50051. The address is a host and a port, with no path. The method goes in the Method field. The address's scheme decides whether Posting connects with TLS:

Address Connection grpc://host:port or http://host:port Plaintext grpcs://host:port or https://host:port TLS localhost:50051, 127.0.0.1:50051 or [::1]:50051 Plaintext, because the host is a loopback address 0.0.0.0:50051 or [::]:50051 Plaintext, because a server that prints this address is listening on this machine Any other address without a scheme, such as api.example.com:8443 TLS unix:///run/app.sock or unix:app.sock Plaintext, over the Unix socket at that path. A relative path is relative to the directory you started Posting in

Without a port, TLS uses port 443 and plaintext uses port 80. If a TLS connection fails because the server only speaks plaintext, the error suggests grpc://. If a plaintext connection fails because the server wants TLS, the error suggests grpcs://.

Verify SSL certificates in the Options tab, and the SSL settings in your configuration, apply as they do to HTTP requests.

The call names the address's host in its :authority header, and over TLS, checks that the server's certificate has that name. A call to a Unix socket names localhost. To use another name, type it in Authority on the Options tab. Use it when you connect through an IP address, a port forward or a load balancer, and the server or its certificate expects its own name. Authority takes variables.

docs.title: The Message and Proto tabs
docs.text:
A gRPC request has two tabs of its own, before the usual ones:

  • Message has the Method field, and the message to send below it.
  • Proto lists the .proto files that describe the server, for servers that don't offer reflection. Leave it empty to ask the server.

The other tabs work as they do for an HTTP request, with these differences:

  • There's no Body, Path or Query tab.
  • The Headers tab is called Metadata. Each enabled row is sent as gRPC metadata, with its name in lower case. A name that ends in -bin takes a base64 value, which Posting decodes before sending. Names that gRPC sets itself (content-type, te, and names that start with grpc- or :) are errors, and so are HTTP/1 headers that HTTP/2 forbids (connection, keep-alive, proxy-connection, transfer-encoding, upgrade and host). A user-agent row replaces Posting's own user agent, and gRPC adds its version after it.
  • Basic and bearer auth are sent as authorization metadata. Digest auth needs an HTTP challenge, so the Auth tab doesn't offer it, and a request file with type: digest doesn't load.
  • The Options tab has Verify SSL certificates, Substitute body variables, Authority and Timeout. The timeout is the deadline for the whole call, including connecting. An open stream uses it only for connecting.

docs.title: Finding methods
docs.text:
Posting contacts a server only when you ask it to. Opening a gRPC request, or showing its tabs, never contacts the server.

When the Proto tab is empty, Posting asks the server's reflection service for its methods. It asks when:

  • The Method field takes focus. Posting asks again only if the address, the metadata or the auth has changed since it last asked, or if that attempt failed.
  • You press Ctrl+R in the Method field, or choose Refresh gRPC methods in the command palette.
  • A send of the request gets a response.

When the server has no reflection service, add its .proto files on the Proto tab instead:

  • Files lists the files, one per line, relative to the collection directory. A file ending in .protoset, .binpb or .pb is a compiled descriptor set, such as protoc --descriptor_set_out or buf build -o writes. Any other file is .proto source, which Posting compiles itself, so you don't need protoc.
  • Import paths lists the directories that import statements are relative to. With none, the collection directory is the only one. Each .proto file must be inside one of them.

With proto files, Posting lists the methods without connecting to the server, so it lists them as soon as the request opens. It reads the files again each time the Method field takes focus, and on Ctrl+R or Refresh gRPC methods, so an edited file is picked up.

The line under the Method field shows how many methods Posting found, and where, for example 4 methods via reflection · plaintext. Once you choose a method, it shows the method's kind and its message types, such as server stream · ListBooksRequest → Book. If Posting couldn't find the methods, the line says why. Before Posting has asked the server, the line says so.

The Method field lists the methods while it has focus, and opens the list when they arrive. Type to filter them, and press Enter to choose one. You can also type a method yourself as package.Service/Method or package.Service.Method.

docs.title: Messages and streams
docs.text:
Write the message as JSON, in protobuf's JSON format: field names in lowerCamelCase or as they're written in the .proto file, enum values by name, and well-known types such as Timestamp in their JSON form. When you choose a method and the message is empty, or still holds the previous method's template, Posting fills it in with a template that has every field of the method's input. Choose Insert gRPC message template in the command palette to replace the message with a template at any time.

What you write depends on the method:

  • A unary or server-streaming method takes one JSON object.
  • A client-streaming or bidirectional method takes a JSON array of objects, and Posting sends each one as a message, in order. A single object is sent as a stream of one message.
  • An empty message is sent as one empty message, for any method.

Variables work as they do in a raw body: $NAME and ${NAME} are both replaced, and typing $ suggests the variables you can use. Turn off Substitute body variables to send the message exactly as written. Press F4 in the message to edit it in your own editor.

When you press Ctrl+J, Posting sends every message and closes its side of the call while it reads the server's replies, so a server that answers each message as it arrives works too. The response shows each reply as it arrives, with RECEIVING in the response panel's title, until the call ends.

docs.title: Open streams
docs.text:
To send messages one at a time while a call runs, open a stream instead. Press Alt+J, or choose Open gRPC stream in the command palette. Posting calls the method, sends the message, and keeps its side of the call open. The response panel's title shows Streaming. While the stream is open:

  • Press Ctrl+J to send the message in the editor. Edit the message between sends to send a different one. For a client-streaming or bidirectional method, a JSON array sends each object as a message. A message that isn't valid for the method shows an error and sends nothing, and the stream stays open.
  • Press Alt+J again, or choose End gRPC stream, to close your side of the call. The server then ends the call when it's ready, as a client-streaming server does when it replies.
  • Press Esc to stop the call at once.

An open stream has no timeout once it has connected. It runs until you end it, you stop it, or the server ends the call. For a unary or server-streaming method, an open stream sends only its first message, and is useful to watch a server stream for longer than the timeout.

docs.title: gRPC responses
docs.text:
The response panel shows the call's status by name, such as OK or NOT_FOUND, with the server's status message beside it. Only OK is shown in the success colour.

The Body tab shows the server's messages as JSON, with fields at their default values included:

  • An object for a unary or client-streaming method.
  • An array for a server-streaming or bidirectional method, even when the server sent one message or none.
  • When the call fails and the server sent no messages, an object with the status's code, message and details. Posting decodes the details whose types it knows, such as the google.rpc error details. It shows the others as their type URL and base64 value.

The Headers tab shows the response metadata. A gRPC response has a Trailers tab instead of Cookies. Trailers arrive when the server ends the call, and they start with grpc-status and, when the server sent one, grpc-message. A call that ends without the server's trailers, such as one that times out, has none.

When a call runs past its timeout, the response shows the messages that arrived before the deadline, with the status DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. When you press Esc after the server has answered, the response keeps the messages that arrived, with the status CANCELLED. When Posting can't reach the server, or the server sends nothing before the deadline, the response panel shows an error, as it does for an HTTP request.

Posting keeps up to 64 MB of messages from a call, the same limit as an HTTP response body. When a stream sends more, Posting cancels the call. The response shows the messages that arrived before the limit, with the status CANCELLED and the message response truncated at 64.00 MB.

Each send opens a new connection to the server. Without proto files, it also asks the server for the method's schema again, so a changed server is picked up straight away.

docs.title: Exporting as grpcurl
docs.text: For a gRPC request, the command palette offers Export as grpcurl in place of Export as curl. The command uses -plaintext or -insecure to match the connection, -unix for a Unix socket, -authority for Authority, -cacert, -cert and -key for the files in your SSL settings when the connection uses TLS, -H for metadata and auth, -d for the message, -max-time for the timeout, and -import-path, -proto and -protoset for the proto files, with absolute paths so the command runs from any directory. Basic and bearer auth replace an authorization metadata row, as they do when Posting sends the request. If the address still has a variable in it, the command keeps the address as written. Only a grpc:// or http:// scheme then makes the command -plaintext, so without a scheme grpcurl uses TLS. grpcurl reads a stream as JSON objects one after another, so an array message is written that way.

docs.title: gRPC request files
docs.text:
A saved gRPC request has kind: grpc and a grpc section instead of a method and a body:

name: Get user
kind: grpc
url: localhost:50051
grpc:
  method: acme.users.v1.UserService/GetUser
  message: |
    {"id": "${USER_ID}"}
  proto:
    files:
      - protos/acme/users/v1/users.proto
    import_paths:
      - protos
auth:
  type: bearer_token
  bearer_token:
    token: ${API_TOKEN}
headers:
  - name: x-tenant
    value: core
options:
  timeout: 10

Leave out the proto section to use reflection. A gRPC request file can't have method, body, params or path_params, and its options can't have follow_redirects, attach_cookies or proxy_url. Any other key in the grpc or proto sections is an error.

Posting 2 doesn't know about gRPC requests. Edit them only in Posting 3.

docs.title: What gRPC requests don't do yet
docs.text:
• gRPC-Web and Connect.
  • Compressed messages.
  • Proxies.
  • Client certificates for a single request. The client certificate in your SSL settings applies to every request.
  • Importing gRPC requests from Postman or grpcurl. Bruno gRPC requests can be imported.
  • Completing proto file paths.
  • Reusing a connection from one send to the next.

docs.title: Sending a request
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+J (or Alt+Enter) from anywhere to send the request in the current tab, or press Enter in the URL bar. Press Esc to cancel it while it's in flight.

Posting sends a User-Agent header identifying itself unless you've set your own. If the URL's address or path, or an OAuth field, uses a variable that isn't defined, Posting tells you which one instead of sending the request. An undefined variable anywhere else, including the query string, is sent as written.

See Responses for what you can do with the response.

docs.title: Saving a request
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+S to save the request in the current tab.

The first time you save a request, Posting asks where to save it:

Field Description Name The request's name. Required. File name The name of the file, without .posting.yaml. Leave it empty to use one made from the name. Folder The folder in the collection to save it in, such as users/admin. Leave it empty to save at the top of the collection. Missing folders are created. Description An optional description.

Press Enter to save. After that, Ctrl+S saves changes to the same file.

docs.title: Renaming a request
docs.text: Change the Name in the Info tab and save. The request keeps its file name; to rename or move the file itself, rename or move it on disk and Posting will notice the change.

docs.title: Duplicating a request
docs.text:
Press D with the cursor on a request in the collection browser, or choose Duplicate request in the command palette, to make a copy. The copy is saved beside the original, with (copy) added to its name, and opened in a new tab.

To duplicate several requests at once, select them first. Their copies aren't opened. They become the selection instead.

docs.title: Deleting a request
docs.text:
Press Backspace with the cursor on a request in the collection browser, or choose Delete request in the command palette to delete the request in the current tab. Posting asks you to confirm, then deletes the file. With several requests selected, Posting asks once and deletes them all.

If the request is open in a tab, the tab stays open with its contents intact, as an unsaved request, so you can save it again if you change your mind.

If your terminal doesn't paste the command in one go, type or paste it and press Enter. A command split over several lines with \ at the end of each line is supported.

You can also:

  • choose Import curl command… in the command palette, and paste the command into the dialog; press Ctrl+J to import it
  • choose Import curl from clipboard to import the command on your clipboard directly (over SSH, this needs a terminal that lets applications read the clipboard)

Importing replaces everything in the current tab's request except its name and description. The request keeps its file too, so importing into a saved request updates it once you save.

Posting understands the options people most often copy from browsers and API docs, including -X, -H, -d and its variants, --json, -F, -u, --digest, -b, -A, -e, -k, -L, -x, -m, -G, -I and --oauth2-bearer. Options that don't affect the request, such as -s, -v and -o, are ignored. A few things to be aware of:

  • -F imports multipart fields, including @path, ;filename= and ;type=. Use separate -F fields for multiple files. --form-string always imports literal text.
  • --data-binary @path and --json @path import a whole-file body. Files are read when sending, so each send uses the current contents. Relative paths resolve against the collection, not the shell directory the command originally ran in. --json supplies JSON Content-Type and Accept headers unless you set them explicitly. A whole-file body cannot be combined with other data fragments or files. Stdin, nested multipart, <file parts and custom per-part headers aren't supported.
  • $NAME in a pasted command isn't expanded: it becomes a Posting variable.

The Values / Variables switch at the top of the dialog chooses between a command with variables replaced by their values (the default), ready to run, or one with the variables left in, ready to share. Press Y to copy the command again.

Uploads export as -F / --form-string, or --data-binary @path for a whole file. Resolved file paths are absolute so the command can run from another directory. Paths with unresolved variables are kept as written. Curl generates the boundary for multipart uploads; empty multipart bodies export with explicit framing instead.

To add your own options to every exported command, set curl_export_extra_args in your configuration:

curl_export_extra_args: "--silent --show-error"

This is inserted straight after curl.

docs.title: Exporting as YAML
docs.text: Choose Export as YAML in the command palette to copy the request in Posting's file format, a quick way to share a request with another Posting user.

docs.title: The request file format
docs.text:
Requests are saved as YAML files ending in .posting.yaml. They're designed to be easy to read, review and edit by hand. Here's an example:

name: Create user
description: Adds a new user to the system.
method: POST
url: https://${API_HOST}/users/:team
body:
  content: |-
    {
      "firstName": "John",
      "email": "john.doe@example.com"
    }
  content_type: application/json
auth:
  type: bearer_token
  bearer_token:
    token: ${API_TOKEN}
headers:
- name: X-Request-ID
  value: docs-example
- name: X-Debug
  value: 'true'
  enabled: false
params:
- name: sendWelcomeEmail
  value: 'true'
path_params:
- name: team
  value: engineering
options:
  timeout: 30

Only settings that differ from the defaults are written, so most files are short:

Key Description name, description Shown in the collection browser and the Info tab. kind graphql for a GraphQL request, grpc for a gRPC request. Left out for an HTTP request. method The HTTP method. Left out for GET. url The URL, without its query string. headers, params Lists of name and value. enabled: false marks a disabled row. path_params The values of the URL's :name placeholders. body One of content for a raw body, form_data for a URL-encoded form, multipart for ordered parts, or file for a whole-file body. Raw and file bodies can also specify content_type. graphql A GraphQL request's query, variables and operation_name. Any other key in it is an error. grpc A gRPC request's method, message and proto (files and import_paths). Any other key in it is an error. auth type is basic, digest, bearer_token or oauth2, with configuration under a key of the same name (basic: {username, password}, bearer_token: {token}). See OAuth 2.0 for oauth2 fields. options Any of follow_redirects, verify_ssl, attach_cookies, substitute_body_variables, proxy_url and timeout. captures Maps session variable names to JSON response paths, e.g. {SESSION_ID: data.id}. See Response captures. scripts Posting 2 scripts. Posting 3 keeps them but doesn't run them; see Scripting.

HTTP requests without OAuth and with none, raw or URL-encoded form bodies use Posting 2's format. OAuth, multipart and file bodies, generated values and response captures require Posting 3.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a response arrives, it's shown in the Response panel. The panel's title shows the status code and reason, coloured green for success, yellow for redirects and red for errors, along with the size of the response and how long it took.

docs.title: Server-sent events (SSE)
docs.text:
Send an ordinary HTTP request to an SSE endpoint. Posting detects Content-Type: text/event-stream and replaces Body with a live Events log. GET and POST both work, including POST requests with a JSON body. Headers, authentication, cookies, TLS settings and variables work as usual; add Accept: text/event-stream if the endpoint requires it.

Events appear as they arrive, with timestamps and event names. Select an event to inspect its data and last event ID; JSON data supports highlighting, search and the JSON tree. Multiline data fields are joined with newlines. Comments are ignored, and an unfinished event isn't dispatched when the connection ends. Gzip and deflate responses are decoded while streaming.

The log follows new events until you move through it or inspect a payload. Arrivals then leave your selection alone and increment the unread count. Press F in the log to follow again. On narrow panels, Enter opens the full-width inspector and Esc returns to the log.

Press Esc from the log to stop the stream. Received events remain available and are saved in history when the stream stops or ends, subject to the usual history size limit. A connection failure keeps the received data and shows Stream interrupted with an error in the log.

In the UI, the request timeout applies until response headers arrive; an established SSE stream stays open until you stop it or the server closes it. Posting does not automatically reconnect or replay a request, and ignores retry fields. Send again to reconnect; add a Last-Event-ID request header if you want the server to resume from a particular event.

For bounded memory use, Posting stops with an explanation if a stream exceeds 10,000 events, 64 MiB of decoded response data, or 1 MiB in a single event or line. The retained raw SSE body is available to exports and posting run --json; headless runs keep their timeout for the entire response and report interruptions as failures.

docs.title: Body
docs.text:
The response body, syntax highlighted based on its Content-Type. JSON, HTML, XML, CSS, JavaScript and YAML are highlighted. JSON is also indented to make it easier to read; to see JSON exactly as the server sent it, set response.prettify_json: false in your configuration.

Move into the body with Down (or jump to it with Ctrl+O then A, then Down) to move through it and select text. The body is read-only, and supports the same Vim-style keys as Posting 2. Below the body, Posting shows its content type, number of lines and, while the body has focus, the cursor's line and column.

Key Action Up Down Left Right / K J H L Move the cursor W / B, Ctrl+Right / Ctrl+Left Next / previous word 0 ^ Home Ctrl+A / $ End Ctrl+E Start / end of the line G / Shift+G Top / bottom of the body % The bracket matching the one under the cursor Page Up Ctrl+B / Page Down Up / down a page Ctrl+U / Ctrl+D Up / down half a page Shift + movement, or Shift+K Shift+J Shift+H Shift+L Shift+W Shift+B Select while moving V Visual mode: moving the cursor selects, as if you were holding Shift. Esc leaves it Shift+V / F6 Select the line F7 Select the whole body Y / C Copy the selection, or the whole body if nothing is selected Ctrl+F / / Find text in the body N / Shift+N Next / previous match while search is open F3 Open the body in your pager F4 Open the body in your editor

You can also click and drag to select, double-click to select a word, and triple-click to select a line. In visual mode, the character under the cursor is part of the selection, as it is in Vim.

Click copy or wrap on/wrap off below the body to copy it or turn line wrapping on or off, or choose Copy response body or Toggle response wrap in the command palette.

docs.title: Searching a response
docs.text:
With the body focused, press Ctrl+F or / to open Find. Matches highlight as you type, and the search bar shows the current match and total, or No matches. Search is literal (not a regular expression) and ignores case.

Press Enter for the next match or Shift+Enter for the previous one; both wrap around at the ends of the body. Press Up to return to the body while keeping search open, then use N and Shift+N to navigate matches, or Y to copy the selected match.

Esc closes search and clears its highlights, leaving the result selected for copying. Reopening Find selects the previous query so you can replace it. Each request tab keeps its own search.

Unlike Posting 2, Ctrl+F opens Find rather than paging down. Use Page Down for a full page or Ctrl+D for half a page (Ctrl+U moves up half a page).

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Responses with an image/* content type open as a preview. Posting supports PNG, JPEG, GIF (the first frame) and static WebP. It also recognises images when the server omits the content type or uses application/octet-stream; explicit text content types stay in the text viewer.

The image fits inside the Body tab without stretching. Terma uses Kitty or Sixel graphics when the terminal supports them, and coloured character cells otherwise. Press Alt+Z to expand the Response panel for a larger preview. The footer shows the decoded format and pixel dimensions.

With the preview focused, press F2 (or click text) to inspect the response as text, and F2 (or preview) to return. Press S or click save to save the original response body bytes, not a screenshot or a re-encoded image. The save dialog accepts absolute or relative paths and ~/; it never overwrites an existing file. These actions also appear in the command palette.

Previews are limited to 32 MiB of encoded data, 16,777,216 pixels and 16,384 pixels per side. Unsupported formats, corrupt images and larger images show an explanation, with text and save still available. Preview errors do not change the HTTP status or response bytes. Images saved in history can be previewed again when you reopen them.

docs.title: JSON tree
docs.text:
For a valid JSON body, click JSON tree below the body or press T while the body has focus. The tree uses Terma's JSON viewer, with collapsible objects and arrays and coloured values. Posting detects JSON from the body even if the server omits or mislabels its content type. The tree also works with responses loaded from history and decoded JSON messages in the gRPC inspector. Empty, malformed and non-JSON bodies keep the text view.

Type an RFC 9535 JSONPath in the field below the tree to filter it, for example $.users[*].name or $.users[?@.admin == true]. Matches keep their ancestors for context and include complete subtrees; array indices refer to the original response. The bar shows the match count. An invalid query displays an error and keeps the last valid results; Esc or × clears the filter.

Key Action Up / Down, K / J Move between nodes Left / Right, H / L Collapse / expand a node Home / End First / last visible node E / Shift+E Expand / collapse all nodes Ctrl+F / / Focus JSONPath, selecting the previous query Enter in JSONPath Return to the tree Y / C Copy the current node's value as JSON, including its complete subtree Shift+Y Copy the current node's JSONPath T Return to the text view

Click Text view or press T to return to text search, selection and wrapping; the text cursor, selection and search are preserved. Each request tab keeps its own view and filter. A new response or selected message clears the filter so it cannot hide the new data. Object keys are sorted in the tree; the text view retains their original order. Copy response body in the command palette and the F3/F4 external tools still use the complete, unfiltered body. Tree rows do not wrap; use the text view to read long values with wrapping enabled.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
The response headers, one per row.

Move into the table with Down, then move between rows with Up / K and Down / J. These keys copy the row under the cursor:

Key Copies Y / C The value N The name B Both, as Name: value

In Headers and Trailers, select several rows with Shift+Up / Shift+Down, Shift-click, or dragging; Ctrl+A selects all. With an explicit selection, Y / C copies the selected rows as Name: value lines, preserving their order and repeated names. Press Esc to clear the selection and return to the single-row shortcuts above.

The same keys work in the Cookies and Trailers tables. B copies a cookie as name=value, the way a Cookie header carries it. The command palette also has Copy header value, Copy header name and Copy header name and value (or cookie or trailer) for the row under the cursor on the tab that's showing.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
The cookies the response set, with each cookie's name, value, path, and whether it's HttpOnly or Secure. Copy a cookie's value with Y, its name with N, or name=value with B. See Headers.

Cookies from responses are remembered until you quit Posting, and sent with later requests to the same site, unless you turn off Attach cookies in the request's Options.

docs.title: Trace
docs.text:
A timeline showing how long each stage of the exchange took:

Stage connect Opening a connection to the server tls handshake Setting up an encrypted connection (skipped for http:// URLs) send headers Sending the request line and headers send body Sending the request body receive headers Waiting for the server, until the response headers arrive receive body Reading the response body response closed Finishing the exchange

The trace is a quick way to see whether a slow request is slow to connect, slow on the server, or slow to download. The same stages are shown as small squares in the URL bar while the request is in flight.

Traces are kept in history, so you can look back at the timing of earlier responses too.

docs.title: Making room
docs.text: Press Alt+Z in the Response panel to expand it to fill the screen, and again to restore it. Layout: side by side in the command palette puts the response beside the request, which suits wide terminals.

docs.title: Responses in other tabs
docs.text: Each request tab keeps its own response. If a response arrives for a tab you're not looking at, it waits in that tab until you go back to it, and every response is added to history.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
posting run sends saved requests without opening the terminal UI or connecting to a running Posting. Agents and scripts can use your existing requests, authentication and environments, then inspect the responses:

posting run api/health.posting.yaml --json
posting run api --env dev --json > results.json
jq -r '.results[0].response.body' results.json

It uses the same HTTP, GraphQL, gRPC and WebSocket clients as the UI, including authentication, TLS settings, uploads, request options and variable substitution. It doesn't open tabs, save history, or change the UI's environment. To send through a Posting someone is watching, use posting remote instead.

docs.title: Working with agents
docs.text:
The bundled using-posting skill teaches agents both commands: use remote when Posting is open beside you, and run for saved requests when no instance is running or when you ask for headless execution. Installing the skill with posting remote skill doesn't require a running instance either.

Use --json so the agent gets response statuses, headers and bodies to work with. Error responses are included too: an exit code of 1 doesn't necessarily mean no response arrived. An agent can inspect a 404, for example, and decide whether it was expected for the task.

This is a request-execution command, not an assertion-based test runner. It can provide basic CI smoke checks, but doesn't verify that a successful response contains the right application data. Custom response assertions are outside its current scope.

docs.title: SSE responses
docs.text: Headless runs can receive server-sent events, but wait for the stream to end rather than print events live. Unlike the UI, the request timeout applies to the whole response. A timeout, interrupted connection or stream size limit fails the request; --json retains the received raw SSE body and includes a streamError explanation. Posting never reconnects automatically.

docs.title: WebSocket requests
docs.text:
A headless WebSocket request sends its saved nonempty message once after connecting, then receives until the server closes or the request timeout expires. An empty draft listens without sending. Normal close codes 1000 and 1001 pass; timeouts, abnormal closes and message/log limits fail while retaining completed messages.

The response body is a JSON array of timestamped log entries. Kind identifies sent/received messages, FrameType identifies text/binary, and Body contains base64-encoded payload bytes (including for text). This preserves binary data and message boundaries in exports. For example:

posting run events.posting.yaml --json | jq -r '.results[0].response.body | fromjson[] | select(.Kind == "received" and .FrameType == "text") | .Body // "" | @base64d'

docs.title: Selecting requests
docs.text:
Give a .posting.yaml file to run one request, or a directory to run every request inside it, recursively. Hidden directories, node_modules and __pycache__ are skipped, just as in the UI. An empty collection is an error, rather than a successful run with no checks.

The collection root is the directory you give, or the parent directory of a single request file. Use --collection (-c) to select a different root. With -c, a relative request or subdirectory path is relative to that root; with no path, the whole collection runs:

posting run -c api users/get.posting.yaml
posting run -c api users
posting run -c api

Upload paths and gRPC schema paths are relative to the collection root, not each request's folder. Use -c when running a nested request that uses files from its parent collection.

Options may appear before or after the path. Unlike remote send, run takes file paths, not request display names, and the .posting.yaml extension is required for a single file.

docs.title: Ordering and dependent requests
docs.text:
Requests run sequentially in case-sensitive lexical order of their relative file paths. This is different from the sidebar, which groups requests by method and display name. Use numbered filenames when order matters, for example:

01-login.posting.yaml
02-create-user.posting.yaml
03-get-user.posting.yaml
04-delete-user.posting.yaml

Cookies carry forward within the run, subject to each request's attach_cookies option. Response captures from successful requests become session variables for subsequent requests, taking precedence over environment and request-scoped values. Failed requests don't update captured values. Cookies and captures are discarded when the run ends.

By default, the runner continues after a failed request and reports every result. Use --fail-fast for dependent sequences so later requests aren't sent after a failure:

posting run api --env dev --fail-fast

Request files are loaded before any request is sent. Unreadable or malformed files, missing URLs, and references to legacy Python scripts abort the run. Posting 3 doesn't execute Python scripts, so run refuses them rather than silently skipping setup or assertions.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Without --env, the runner loads posting.env and posting.local.env from the collection root. It never uses the UI's remembered environment or implicitly loads environment files from the current working directory or Posting's config directory.

--env NAME (-e NAME) looks up a named environment in the collection root and applies the usual layers: posting.env, posting.local.env, NAME.env, NAME.local.env, skipping missing files. An explicit file path is relative to the current working directory and loads just that file. Repeat --env to layer names or files, with later values winning:

posting run api --env dev --env ./overrides.env

Use environment files to refer to secrets supplied by your shell, rather than putting credentials on the command line or committing them:

# api/dev.env
BASE_URL="${DEV_API_URL}"
API_TOKEN="${DEV_API_TOKEN}"

Posting's config.yaml and POSTING_* shell settings still apply, including custom CA bundles, client certificates and use_host_environment. With POSTING_USE_HOST_ENVIRONMENT=true, shell variables are available directly to requests, beneath environment-file values. Invalid settings abort the run instead of silently falling back to defaults. Settings aren't loaded from .env files.

docs.title: Results and exit codes
docs.text:
Text output gives one line per request and a summary. It doesn't print response headers or bodies:

PASSED 01-health.posting.yaml: 200 OK (3.42 ms)
FAILED 02-users.posting.yaml: 503 Service Unavailable
1 passed, 1 failed, 0 skipped
Exit code Meaning 0 Every request passed. 1 A request failed, the run was interrupted, or its files/configuration couldn't be loaded. 2 Invalid command-line arguments.

HTTP 4xx/5xx responses, GraphQL responses with errors, non-OK gRPC statuses, transport errors, timeouts and failed response captures count as failures. Redirects aren't failures; requests follow them unless their follow_redirects option is disabled. Request timeouts also bound gRPC streams; there's no interactive stream mode in a headless run.

These are status checks, not custom assertions about your API's response. A 200 with the wrong application data still passes unless a declared capture fails. Inspect the JSON response to determine whether it meets the task's expectations. remote send keeps its different exit behavior: receiving any response is a success, even an error status.

--json prints one JSON document with results, passed, failed and skipped. Results are in execution order, each with file, name, outcome (passed or failed), an error on failure, and a response if one arrived. The response fields match remote send --json, including status, headers, trailers, elapsed time, and a textual body or bodyBase64 for non-UTF-8 data. Setup errors also appear in the report's top-level error field. Argument errors print usage diagnostics on stderr instead of a JSON report.

posting run api --env dev --json > results.json
jq '.results[] | {file, outcome, error, status: .response.status}' results.json
jq -r '.results[0].response.body' results.json

Reports may contain secrets

JSON reports contain response headers and bodies, which can include tokens, cookies or private data. Error messages can also include request URLs. Don't publish them as unrestricted artifacts or logs. Text output omits response bodies, but is not a secret-redaction mechanism.

Only run collections you trust, against an appropriate test environment: running a collection sends every selected request, including requests that modify data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Posting 2 could run Python scripts before a request was sent and after its response arrived, to set variables, change the request, or log information.

Posting 3 doesn't run scripts. It's a single binary written in Go, with no Python inside it to run them with.

docs.title: Requests with scripts
docs.text:
Requests saved by Posting 2 can refer to scripts in their scripts section:

scripts:
  setup: scripts/setup.py
  on_request: scripts/auth.py:sign_request
  on_response: scripts/extract_token.py

Posting 3 opens these requests and sends them without running the scripts. The scripts section is kept when you save the request, so you can go on using the same collection with Posting 2 without losing anything.

The headless runner, posting run, rejects requests with scripts before sending anything, so required setup or response processing isn't silently omitted.

If you rely on scripts, Posting 2 remains available and reads the same collections, so you can use both side by side.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
Some common uses of scripts can be handled without them in Posting 3:

With a script, you'd… In Posting 3 Set a variable for later requests Set a session value on the variables screen (Ctrl+Shift+V) Generate an idempotency key or timestamp for each send Use generated values, such as ${$uuid} Extract a token or ID from a response Declare response captures in the request file Choose values per environment Use layered environment files Read secrets from somewhere else Refer to shell variables from your environment files, e.g. API_TOKEN="${STAGING_TOKEN}", or turn on use_host_environment Add authentication Use the Auth tab with variables, e.g. a Bearer token of ${API_TOKEN} Keep a copy of responses Every response is kept in history

Scripting may return in a future version. See the roadmap.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Posting 3 comes with 37 built-in themes, and can load themes you make yourself, including the themes you made for Posting 2.

docs.title: Choosing a theme
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+P and choose Theme… to see every theme. As you move through the list, Posting previews each one, so you can see how it looks before you choose it. Press Enter to use the highlighted theme, or Esc to go back to the theme you had.
